notes:
I've written notes for most verses. I ran out of research tools before some later and comparison sources loaded, so the gaps are listed at the end. Everything is in my own words, and each point gives its source URL.

---

## Matthew 23: research notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Jesus speaks *to* the crowds and disciples but *about* the scribes and Pharisees. He was done addressing those opponents and now meant to warn the people and His followers about them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- Precept Austin calls this Jesus' last public sermon, preached in the Temple shortly before the cross. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the leaders were to be respected for their office, not their conduct, because they held an authority God had ordained. He cites Carson that synagogues had a stone seat at the front for the teacher. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- Precept Austin: rabbis sat to teach, and "Moses' seat" stands for authority to teach and interpret the Law. Its summary: they took Moses' seat but not his spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary
- The NET Bible note (quoted on Precept Austin) says "scribes" were experts in the law of Moses and in traditional rules, so "expert in the law" is clearer for modern readers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**v. 3**
- GotQuestions (quoted on Precept Austin): obey the leaders' teaching insofar as they taught God's law, but don't copy their behaviour. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary
- Spurgeon (Baptist, quoted on Precept Austin): they were to be obeyed only as far as they truly followed Moses. Jesus could not have meant the people to accept their false add-ons to the Law, since He had already said their traditions cancelled God's commandment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**v. 4**
- Guzik contrasts the leaders with Jesus, whose burden is light (Matt 11:30): they loaded burdens on people, while Jesus takes burdens away. He links this to Peter's rejection of legalism in Acts 15:10 and warns that many teachers today still present Christianity as a set of heavy rules. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/

**v. 5**
- Guzik: phylacteries (small leather boxes holding Scripture, tied to arm and head) and garment borders were God's commands (Deut 11:18; Num 15:38–40). Using them to look extra-spiritual was human sin, not a fault in the command. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- Matthew Henry (quoted on Precept Austin) says the Pharisees made these larger than usual to seem more zealous, and that pride was their chief sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: they were not content to look spiritual; they wanted to be admired for it. He cites Poole that the stress falls on "love": accepting such honours for the sake of civil order might be fine, but craving them is not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/

**vv. 8–10: where traditions differ ("Rabbi", "father", "instructor")**
- Traditional background: Ellicott says "Abba" (father) was a title the scribes loved. Jesus' point was not to honour human fathers so much that people forget God's fatherhood. https://biblehub.com/matthew/23-9.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says "father" was given to famous teachers and founders of schools. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html
- **Evangelical (Calvary Chapel, Guzik):** not an absolute ban, since inspired writers used these titles (Paul calls himself a father in 1 Cor 4:15). The target is a heart that loves titles. Guzik still says the command is widely broken today, and gives the formal closing for letters to the Pope as an example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- **Reformed (Calvin):** God alone holds the honour of Father in this sense. But calling earthly men fathers is lawful, and refusing them that honour would actually be wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html
- **Baptist (Gill):** children may call parents fathers, and converts may call those who led them to faith spiritual fathers. What Jesus rejects is titles claiming authority over people's consciences. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** Jesus is probably alluding to the "Ab" (father) of the Sanhedrin, its second-ranking officer. The point is that Jesus wanted no second-in-command after Himself in the Church, and perfect equality among His followers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html
- **Stricter readings:** Coffman (Restoration Movement) says Christ condemned religious titles that denote authority, and forbade both accepting and giving them. He criticises calling priests "father". Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says he cannot bring himself to address Catholic or Episcopal ministers as "father" because Jesus said not to. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers notes that a few verses later (v. 32) Jesus Himself says "your fathers", so v. 9 forbids the *misuse* of the title, not the word. https://www.catholic.com/qa/how-can-we-explain-calling-priests-father-when-jesus-said-not-to
- Another Catholic article says Jesus condemns taking over God's fatherhood, not sharing in it. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/fatherly-wisdom
- On a Catholic Answers broadcast, Trent Horn says priests are called "Father" because they are spiritual fathers. https://www.catholic.com/video/why-do-catholics-call-priests-father-if-the-bible-says-call-no-man-father
- **Orthodox:** I found no oca.org source. The only mention is a Protestant commentary (Preacher's Homiletical) remarking that Greek Church parish priests are called "Papa". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-9.html

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik: the world measures greatness by how many serve you, Jesus' kingdom by how you serve others. Jesus, truly the greatest, called Himself a servant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- Bible Hub's study page notes that the Greek word here is *diakonos*, "servant". https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/matthew/23.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: "hypocrite" literally means an actor playing a part. The leaders shut the kingdom by putting human tradition above God's Word, which showed in their rejection of Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- GotQuestions: the door into the kingdom is repentance and faith in Christ, which the self-justifying Pharisees disliked most. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html
- On the word "woe": Lenski (Lutheran, quoted on Precept Austin) says it states a fact, not a wish. It is a calm verdict from the supreme Judge, not a curse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary
- Barclay says the Greek *ouai* carries both wrath and sorrow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/matthew-23.html

**v. 14 (text question)**
- Guzik quotes Carson that the verse is a later addition: it is missing from the best early manuscripts, and the manuscripts that have it disagree on where it goes. The same saying does appear in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- Kelly lists the ancient manuscripts that leave it out and suggests it was copied in from Mark and Luke, which leaves seven woes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/23-13.html
- On its meaning, Guzik and Spurgeon take "greater condemnation" to show there are degrees of punishment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: zeal in winning converts didn't prove they were right with God (compare Rom 10:2). He cites Barclay that a proselyte was a full convert who accepted circumcision, and Carson that the first century was a high point of Jewish missionary zeal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- GotQuestions: they led converts into a religion of works, not true righteousness. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html

**vv. 16–22**
- GotQuestions: rather than teach spiritual truth, they argued over trivia and looked for loopholes. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html
- Bible Hub's study page ties this to Matt 5:34–37 ("let your yes be yes"): God hears every word, and no formula reduces accountability. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/matthew/23.htm
- Bible Hub's topical entry says Jesus exposes them for valuing material wealth over what is truly holy. https://biblehub.com/topical/t/the_seven_woes.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Bible Hub's study page: the Law of Moses did require tithing produce (Lev 27:30). https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/matthew/23.htm
- GotQuestions: they counted out mint leaves but ignored justice, mercy and faithfulness. "Gnat and camel" is deliberate exaggeration: careful over tiny matters while tolerating great sins. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html

**vv. 25–26**
- Guzik: they cared a great deal about outward appearance and not at all about the sin inside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- GotQuestions: their religious practice made them look clean while their hearts were full of greed. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html

**vv. 27–28**
- Guzik: Jews whitewashed tombs before Passover so no one would touch one by accident and become ritually unclean. The leaders were pretty outside and dead inside, and God sees what we really are. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/

**vv. 29–31**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** he rejects the view that Jesus is condemning superstitious honour of the dead. The fault was hypocrisy: winning public favour by honouring dead prophets while persecuting living ones. Calvin applies this sharply against the Roman Church of his day. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html
- GotQuestions: by talking about "our fathers" they admitted their family line, and they had inherited its wickedness. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-woes.html
- A. T. Robertson (quoted on Precept Austin) mentions monuments called Tombs of the Prophets at the foot of the Mount of Olives, some perhaps being built at that very time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**v. 32**
- Calvin: this is not a command to kill. It is a figure of speech saying they will finish what their fathers began, and a warning to ordinary people not to be surprised when God's prophets are mistreated. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html

**v. 33**
- Calvin: the harsh language was needed to shake off hypocrites' self-flattery. It was aimed at the whole people as a warning, and the punishment applies unless they repent quickly. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html

**v. 34**
- Calvin compares Luke's "the Wisdom of God said" and takes it as God speaking through the prophets. He gives a clearly Reformed reading: God sometimes sends His word to people He knows will refuse it, which leaves them without excuse. He adds that a faithful remnant is always excepted. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html

**v. 35**
- Calvin: "you" covers the whole nation through its history. Because every generation joined the same rebellion, it is just for the guilt to fall on the children too. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html

**v. 36**
- Stu Weber (quoted on Precept Austin): take "this generation" literally, since judgment came on Israel in the AD 70 destruction. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-23-commentary

**v. 37: where traditions differ (God's will and human refusal)**
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Christ could only say this about longing across the ages if He were more than a man. The verse also shows that people's ruin lies with themselves. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/i-would-but-ye-would-not/
- **Baptist, Calvinist (Gill):** Jesus speaks here with a human will and wish for Jerusalem's earthly good. This does not contradict God's sovereign will. Gill also stresses that it was the rulers ("ye") who refused, not the children Jesus wanted to gather. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/matthew/23-37.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** the words show indignation toward the scribes more than compassion. The "will" meant here is God's revealed will, calling everyone through preaching, not His secret purpose. Those God effectively means to gather, He draws inwardly by His Spirit. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom33.ii.xiii.html
- **Evangelical (Guzik):** behind all the woes is Jesus' real love for these people. He spoke harshly to warn them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-23/
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers uses this verse against Calvinism. As God, Jesus truly willed to gather them and they refused, so grace can be resisted. It cites the Catechism (§600): God's plan of predestination includes each person's free response. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/predestined-for-freedom and https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/gods-resistible-grace

**v. 38**
- Coffman: some scholars omit "desolate", but the meaning holds either way. This was the end of Jesus' last public discourse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/matthew-23.html

---

**What I couldn't find:**
- **v. 39:** I have no notes on "until you say, Blessed is He…", including the debate over whether it points to a future turning of Israel. Calvin's page cut off before he reached it.
- **v. 35:** nothing on who "Zechariah son of Berechiah" was. The same cut-off happened on the Abel/Zechariah section.
- **Missing perspectives:**
  - Wesley's own notes on v. 37 (Adam Clarke is the only Methodist voice here, on v. 9)
  - Pentecostal or charismatic sources
  - Lutheran sources other than Lenski's line on "woe"
  - Orthodox sources (oca.org)
  - Bible Odyssey, or NET notes beyond the one on "scribes"
  - Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on v. 23 or elsewhere

A follow-up pass could target v. 35, v. 39 and those missing perspectives.
